case.subject: Incident review
case.title: Payment API outage postmortem and actions

canvasName: R3-C07 Payment API outage postmortem and actions

segments.text: This is the postmortem for the payment API outage on Tuesday. The incident lasted fifty two minutes, from 14:07 to 14:59 UTC. During that window, about sixty percent of card payments failed, and some customers saw a generic error page. No money was lost, but we violated our error budget for the quarter and we need to understand both the technical cause and the process gaps. This meeting is blameless.
segments.textReply: Captured the outage timeline, customer impact, financial outcome, quarterly error-budget breach, and blameless review goals.

segments.text: We are here to find system problems, not to assign personal fault. Let's build the timeline. At 13:55, we deployed release 4.18.2, which included a small change to the connection pool settings. At 14:03, the first alert fired for elevated latency on the payment service. At 14:07, error rate crossed five percent. The on call engineer acknowledged at 14:09 and began checking dashboards.
segments.textReply: I’m adding the four confirmed milestones, keeping the sequence factual and blame-free.

segments.text: At 14:14, the team saw database connection timeouts. At 14:21, they rolled back the release, but the error rate did not recover. At 14:32, they discovered that the DNS resolver was returning a stale address for one of the primary database replicas. At 14:41, they failed over to the secondary replica and traffic recovered. At 14:59, error rate returned to baseline and the incident was closed.
segments.textReply: Adding the remaining milestones in a second column, including the rollback that did not restore service and the eventual recovery path.

segments.text: The direct cause was a combination of two changes. The release reduced the connection pool timeout from five seconds to two seconds, which made the service less tolerant of slow DNS. Separately, a network change on Monday had reduced the DNS cache TTL, so the resolver was more likely to return stale records during a failover. The stale record pointed to a replica that had been taken out of service.
segments.textReply: The cause combines a tighter pool timeout with more frequent DNS refreshes, exposing a stale record for a retired replica.

segments.text: The service kept retrying the stale address, and the shortened timeout turned a slowdown into a hard failure. Why did the rollback not fix it? Because the DNS record was already cached, and the rollback did not flush the resolver cache. The team assumed the release was the only change. The runbook said to roll back first, then check dependencies, but it did not say to verify DNS after a rollback.
segments.textReply: I’m adding the failure mechanism and the two process gaps: cached DNS persisted, and the runbook omitted DNS verification.

segments.text: That is a process gap. The on call had the authority to fail over, but they waited for the database team because the runbook described failover as a last resort. That added about nine minutes. Detection was also slower than it should have been. The latency alert fired at 14:03, but it was a warning, not a page. The error rate alert paged at 14:07. We had no synthetic check for card payments from an external region.
segments.textReply: This adds two response gaps: delayed failover escalation and detection coverage that lacked a paging latency alert and external payment check.Added the response and detection gaps: failover was delayed about nine minutes while awaiting the database team, latency alerts were warning-only, and no external-region synthetic card-payment check existed.

segments.text: The dashboard showed service level error rate, but not the percentage of payment attempts that never reached the service. If we had a synthetic payment probe, we might have caught the failure at 14:05. Customer impact. About eighteen thousand payment attempts failed. Most were retried successfully within ten minutes. Four hundred customers saw a duplicate authorization hold, which we reversed automatically by 16:30.
segments.textReply: I’ll add the newly quantified customer outcomes and the visibility gap, including the estimated 14:05 synthetic detection point.

segments.text: Support received two hundred and ten tickets. The status page was updated at 14:26, nineteen minutes after the incident started. That is too slow. We need a template and a designated communications owner. Now the contributing factors. First, the config change was not covered by a canary in the payment path. Second, the DNS dependency was not in the service map.
segments.textReply: Adding the customer-support and communications delay, then recording the two contributing system gaps.

segments.text: Third, the runbook did not include cache invalidation or DNS verification. Fourth, the failover decision required a second team, which added latency. Fifth, the status page update was manual and owned by whoever was on call. Sixth, the alert thresholds were tuned for a single region, not for the payment path as a whole. The action items need owners and dates.

segments.text: First, add a synthetic payment probe that runs from two regions every minute. Owner is the reliability team, due in two weeks. Second, add DNS health to the payment service dashboard and include resolver cache checks in the runbook. Owner is the platform team, due in one week. Third, change the connection pool timeout back to five seconds and add a canary that runs for thirty minutes before full rollout.

The third action’s owner and due date are still unspecified.

shapes.title: Post-session summary · Payment API outage
shapes.html:
Payment API outage · Tuesday postmortem

Purpose: Blameless review of the 52-minute payment outage, technical cause, customer impact, and system/process improvements.

Core mechanism & decisions

Release 4.18.2 shortened the connection-pool timeout 5s → 2s, reducing tolerance for slow DNS. A Monday network change reduced DNS cache TTL; stale DNS pointed to a retired DB replica. Retries kept using the cached address, so rollback alone did not recover service. Failover restored traffic.

Agreed: Sev 1; quarterly error budget exhausted. Payment-path feature changes require reliability review per policy—not punishment. Keep incident-channel structure and automatic duplicate-hold reversal. Review actions weekly until closed.

Compact timeline · UTC

13:55 deploy · 14:03 latency warning · 14:07 errors >5% · 14:09 on-call acknowledges · 14:14 DB timeouts · 14:21 rollback, no recovery · 14:32 stale DNS found · 14:41 failover · 14:59 baseline / close.

Impact: ~60% card payments failed; ~18,000 attempts failed, most retried within 10 minutes. 400 duplicate holds were reversed by 16:30; no money lost. 210 support tickets. Status page first updated 14:26.

Action register

ActionOwnerDeadline
Synthetic payment probe, two regions, every minuteReliability team2 weeks
DNS health dashboard + resolver-cache runbook checksPlatform team1 week
Restore 5s timeout; 30-minute canary before full rolloutPayments team3 days
Explicit on-call failover authority; update escalation policyEngineering manager1 week
Status-page template + communications rotationSupport2 weeks
Post-deploy DNS verification in release checklistRelease Engineering2 weeks
Design resolver sidecar or TTL-independent service discovery; RFC, design onlyPlatform team6 weeks

Process commitments

5-minute pre-deploy DNS + DB health check; canary for timeout, pool, or retry changes; one incident commander for every Sev 1; first status-page update target: 15 minutes. Follow-up review in 2 weeks checks synthetic probe, runbook, canary, and status template.

Open risks & follow-up

Dashboard missed payment attempts that never reached the service; synthetic probe might have detected failure by 14:05. Alerting was warning-only at 14:03 and scoped to a single region; DNS was absent from the service map. Runbook omitted DNS verification/cache invalidation; failover waited ~9 minutes for another team. Owners should flag any likely slip before Friday. RFC is design-only; implementation plan remains open. Process-change action owners/dates were not specified.
